To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

dog sports are a serious leisure pursuit, that they are a culture of commitment, that they generate strong behavioural expectations that clash with expectations from the real world, and that when this happens respondents negotiate between the two sets of demands.
the culture of commitment of serious leisure can be seen as a boundary object that is both shaped by and shapes the boundaries of work, family and other institutions.

1) dog sports are a ‘culture of serious leisure’; 2) this culture is a ‘world’ that shapes the lives of its participants; 3) this ‘world’ interfaces with the ‘world’ of the ‘real’; 4) the interface is characterized by boundary negotiations that simultaneously reproduce and reshape both the serious leisure world and the world of the ‘real’.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how people negotiate the boundaries between serious leisure and the real world.
the boundary negotiations between serious leisure, work, family, and other institutions.
how people negotiate between the demands of serious leisure, and those of the ‘world outside’.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
dog sports are a serious leisure activity that shapes and reshapes the meanings of life for participants.
serious leisure is a ‘boundary negotiation’ activity.
dog sports is a serious leisure pursuit that is a world of its own.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the ‘real world’, including work, family and religious life, is not a monolithic force that shapes people's life meanings, but rather a set of institutions with which people interact and negotiate, sometimes in conflict, sometimes in harmony.
dog sports participants, like other serious leisure hobbyists, have created a culture of commitment.
dog sports participants are not just ‘serious leisure’ hobbyists.
The main takeaway from our work is that
leisure is not simply a matter of ‘having fun’; it can be a serious business that shapes people's lives in important ways.
leisure can indeed be a ‘world’ with its own rules and values, and one that is as important as the ‘real world‘ for the people who participate in it.
leisure is not just a ‘haven’ from the ‘real world’, but a ‘world’ of its own that shapes the meanings and practices of other social institutions.
